# Build For Good — full reference

> Build For Good is a global, multidisciplinary community for turning meaningful problems into collective action — exceptional people across every field, building things that matter, together.

This file is a plain-text consolidation of the public Build For Good website for
LLM ingestion. Canonical origin: https://buildforgood.world

Motto: Build. Grow. Evolve. Together.
Founder & Steward: Nikhil Nagpure.
Contact: hello@buildforgood.world
GitHub: https://github.com/webuildforgood

---

## What Build For Good is

Build For Good (BFG) is a global, multidisciplinary community. It brings
together genuine, ambitious, curious and compassionate people who want to become
more capable without becoming less human, and turns meaningful problems into
collective action.

It is deliberately multidisciplinary. Engineering, medicine, science, design,
law, policy, philosophy and the skilled trades meet on real work — not only in
name. The design principle is simple: a mathematician, a doctor, a civil
engineer and a security researcher see a problem in ways no single discipline
can, so they are put in the same room and asked to build.

It is open to problems and selective with people. Anyone, anywhere can submit a
problem through the Problem Commons. Membership is earned through an
application, a conversation and a 30-day trial, and is judged by conduct, not
credentials.

North Star: become more capable without becoming less human.
This is not a networking farm, not a self-promotion channel, and not any one
founder's startup — Build For Good belongs to its members.

## What the name means

- Build — build things that matter; move from idea → action → experiment →
  real-world impact.
- Grow — grow intellectually, technically, emotionally and ethically.
- Evolve — question your assumptions, accept criticism, change your mind when
  the evidence demands it.
- Together — collective intelligence accomplishes what isolated individuals
  cannot. Different disciplines, one problem.

## Disciplines

Mathematics · Physics · Medicine & health · Engineering · Software & AI ·
Cybersecurity · Business & entrepreneurship · Strategy & policy · Philosophy ·
Design & art · Law · Environment · Education · Agriculture · Skilled trades —
and fields that do not exist yet.

## Values (how members behave, not what they claim)

Each value is written twice: the behaviour rewarded, and the behaviour corrected.

1. Character before capability — reward people who keep promises, admit
   mistakes early, and do the right thing when it costs them; correct brilliance
   used as a licence and status used as a shield.
2. Intellectual humility — reward "I don't know", "I was wrong", "can you
   explain that to me?"; correct performing expertise, dismissing questions,
   one-upmanship, citing credentials instead of reasoning.
3. Constructive disagreement — reward attacking the idea, steelmanning the
   other side, changing your mind publicly; correct personal attacks, sarcasm as
   a weapon, pile-ons, arguing to win.
4. Generosity as a default — reward answering questions, reviewing work, making
   introductions, sharing resources, crediting others; correct hoarding
   knowledge, gatekeeping, showing up only to ask for something.
5. Follow-through — reward shipping, small consistent contributions, closing
   the loop, saying no instead of ghosting; correct enthusiasm followed by
   disappearance.
6. Respect for people and planet — reward kindness to newcomers, patience with
   different skill levels, environmental and social awareness; correct cruelty
   disguised as directness, exploitation, building harm and calling it progress.
7. Ownership without empire-building — reward "I'll take care of that" and
   actually doing it; correct seeking authority without service, treating
   members as an audience or a workforce.
8. Privacy and trust — reward keeping confidences and handling personal data
   carefully; correct sharing member details or recruiting people out without
   consent.

Culture test before sending anything: (1) would I stand by this if it were
screenshotted and shown to everyone here? (2) does this make Build For Good more
or less the place exceptional people choose to stay? If either answer is no,
don't send it.

## Membership — the twelve dimensions

Membership is open to meaningful problems and selective with people. We choose
small and excellent over fast and ordinary.

The twelve dimensions we judge each other by:

- Character (a gate, not an average) — keep promises, even when it costs
- Kindness — make people feel respected and safe
- Curiosity — ask better questions than you answer
- Ambition — set real goals, show consistent effort
- Competence — show what you've built or done
- Humility — "I don't know", accepts correction
- Critical thinking — question your own assumptions
- Collaboration — make others better
- Responsibility — think through consequences before acting
- Discipline — follow through, repeatedly
- Growth mindset — use criticism as fuel
- Positive intent — want capability to create, not to dominate

Scoring: each dimension is scored 1–5. Anyone scoring 1–2 on Character is
declined regardless of every other score. Otherwise, Character must be ≥ 4 and
the average of the remaining dimensions must be ≥ 3.

The process:

1. Apply — under ten minutes. No CV and no years-of-experience field, by
   design. We ask what you have built and one thing you are struggling with.
2. Talk — a 15–20 minute voice conversation. Not an interrogation; you are
   deciding whether we are worth your time too.
3. Trial — membership is provisional for 30 days. Introduce yourself, help
   someone, show up once; then it is confirmed.

Three doors, so everyone finds theirs in one screen:

- Bring a problem — open to anyone, anywhere, because problems need solving,
  not permission.
- Join Build For Good — application → conversation → 30-day trial.
- Join a Lab — contributing to a problem never requires membership; some work
  needs domain expertise, some needs translation.

Full membership page: https://buildforgood.world/membership

## Problem Commons

The world has no shortage of problems — only a shortage of people willing and
capable of solving them, across disciplines, borders and status. Anyone,
anywhere can submit a problem. Submit: https://buildforgood.world/problems#submit

The loop: Submit → Understand → Assemble → Lab → Validate → Deploy → Impact →
Share. Is it real and who is affected? Which disciplines does it actually need?
A small Lab team researches, designs, prototypes and tests in the wild, then
asks whether it works outside a document, whether it can be implemented where
the affected people are, who benefited, and what was learned. No problem in, no
loop.

The capacity rule and promise:
- Every submission gets a human answer within 72 hours.
- Every submission is framed, parked, or declined with a reason.
- If submissions outpace reviews, intake is closed honestly rather than left
  unanswered. An unanswered submission is a broken promise; a closed door is not.
- Build For Good does not promise to solve your problem; it promises to help
  determine whether, how, and with whom it can be meaningfully worked on.

How problems are chosen — no upvotes, ever (voting picks popularity, not
importance). Each submission is weighed on: Severity; People affected (how
many, and how underserved); Urgency; Neglectedness (is anyone credible already
on it?); Feasibility; Expertise available; Testability; Scalability; and
Safety & ethics.

Lifecycle stages shown for every problem: Submitted → Reviewed → Framed →
Research → Lab forms → Prototype → Pilot → Deployment → Impact → Learn.
Paused and archived are honest endings. Stage 10 — what worked, what failed,
what the next team should know — is mandatory.

Full Problem Commons page: https://buildforgood.world/problems

## Activities — the recurring rituals

A manifesto does not make people stay; something happening does. Five recurring
formats, run as rituals rather than one-offs.

- Build Night — Weekly · 90 minutes · voice + screen share. 10 min kickoff →
  60 min building together → 20 min show-and-tell. Anything counts: automation,
  a website, a CLI tool, a cyber lab, a hardware prototype, an NGO site. No
  spectators — everyone builds something.
- Deep Dive — Weekly or fortnightly · 20–30 minutes. One member presents
  something they are obsessed with: 25 min talk → 15 min genuine Q&A, recorded.
  Anyone can speak, including week-one members; the host role rotates.
- Challenge — Fortnightly · one week · teams of 2–4. A small collaborative
  problem with a deadline, announced Monday and demoed Sunday. Judged on
  usefulness, effort and collaboration — not polish.
- Think — Weekly · async-first. A question worth arguing about well runs all
  week so time zones do not kill it. One person steelman-moderates and posts
  the best opposing arguments before it closes. The goal is to think better
  together, not to win.
- Impact — Monthly · physical or measurable. Tree planting, local cleanups,
  free teaching, software for an NGO, open-source maintenance — measured and
  reported ("we planted 40 trees with 9 people" beats "we did good").

Quarterly and milestone rhythms: Showcase (quarterly — every active project
demos); Retreat / Meetup (2× per year); Charter Review (quarterly — members
propose changes to the rules); Project Retros (end of each project); New Member
Cohort (monthly — admit and onboard in small batches).

Rituals are launched gradually — Build Night first, then Think, then Deep Dive,
then Challenge, then Impact — so participation stays real. If only one could be
kept alive, keep Build Night.

Full activities page: https://buildforgood.world/activities

## Projects

The public record of what members are actually making — tools, research,
prototypes and small services built for real people, at every stage from idea to
scaled. Nothing is aspirational marketing: projects are submitted by members and
reviewed by a human before they are published, and each shows its stage, the
people behind it, where it is rooted, and the links to explore it.

How it works: Submit → Review → Published. A member sends a project (title, a
one-line summary, what it is, its stage, and links); a person reviews whether it
is real, whether the description is honest, and whether it is the member's work
to show; approved projects appear in the public showcase.

Projects are not ranked and vanity metrics are not chased. The point is to make
the work visible, connect the people who can help, and let others learn from
what worked and what did not. Projects usually begin with a problem worth
solving.

Full projects page: https://buildforgood.world/projects

## Founders & roles

One person started Build For Good; it is not meant to stay one person's work.
Titles describe accountability, not status. Where a role has no holder, that is
stated plainly — an honest gap beats a borrowed name.

- Founder — Nikhil Nagpure (filled). Owns the culture, the long view, and the
  promise that every submission gets a human answer. Accountable for staying
  small enough to stay honest and for setting no direction alone.
- Stewards (open) — moderation, onboarding, hosting and mentoring. Earned,
  never appointed; if a Steward stops showing up, the title goes with the
  behaviour.
- Guides (open) — field knowledge: clinicians, engineers, researchers, designers
  and tradespeople who review real work in their discipline, kindly.
- Members & contributors (open to join) — the actual building: research,
  prototypes, translation, field work, documentation, follow-through.
  Contribution is bigger than code.

There is no CTO, no advisory board and no stock team page. Every person shown
exists and does the thing.

Full founders page: https://buildforgood.world/founders

## About

A global network turning problems into action, founded by Nikhil Nagpure and
built by everyone who contributes. The image the community presents is honest:
no invented team, no borrowed titles — an honest "nobody yet" beats a grid of
stock smiles.

Full about page: https://buildforgood.world/about
